pack.name: The sabbatical
pack.description: Rules for taking a deliberate break from paid work, testing an idea before committing to it, and coming back to a market that moved. The figures are modelling assumptions, not predictions: one month of costs is set at 1,200 in the effect reasons, and every number is visible in the node the rule produces.

rules.label: A month of the real thing, unpaid
rules.summary: You take four weeks away from paid work to do the thing properly: the course, the prototype, the client work. Money goes out and nothing comes in, but the question stops being hypothetical.
rules.detail: The value is not the month itself. It is finding out whether the work is worth the sacrifice while the decision is still reversible.

effects.reason: one month of living costs with no income
a break from the current load
a tested alternative is a real one
a month of evidence instead of speculation

assumptions: One month of costs is modelled at 1,200; the effect list shows that figure rather than hiding it in a total.
uncertainties: A good month is not the same as a good year, and the novelty may be doing some of the work.

evidence.text: The costs and the information gained are stated modelling choices, not measured outcomes.

gains: Evidence about the work before a permanent commitment.
A real rest, which is a result even if the idea fails.
costs: One month of income and the security it bought.
A month is short enough to be misleading in either direction.

nextSteps: Decide before the month starts what evidence would make you continue and what would make you stop.
failurePoints: Treating the month as a holiday and calling the lack of evidence a verdict.

rules.label: The break runs out of money before it runs out of plans
rules.summary: Three months was the plan. By the second month the buffer is doing the deciding: the cheap version of the project replaces the useful version, and the return date moves closer.

effects.reason: money decides the plan instead of you
the return date is no longer yours to choose
the useful version of the work was cut

assumptions: A thin buffer forces cheaper choices before it forces a return to work.
uncertainties: Whether the cheaper version is genuinely worse, or only feels that way under pressure.

evidence.text: Modelled as pressure changing the choice, not as a probability that the money runs out.

gains: The experiment still happens, at a smaller scale.
costs: The result is confounded by the shortage rather than by the idea.

nextSteps: Write down the minimum viable version before the money makes the decision for you.
failurePoints: Borrowing to keep the original plan alive without changing the plan.

rules.label: The time away changes the question
rules.summary: You come back with a different answer than the one you left with. That is not a failure of the plan; it is the plan working.

effects.reason: the goal is now chosen with evidence
a second route is now credible
the question is settled for now

assumptions: Enough evidence has accumulated that the preference survives contact with the work.
uncertainties: A changed answer may reflect the break rather than the work; the two are hard to separate.

evidence.text: The rule only becomes available after information has accumulated; it does not claim the new answer is correct.

gains: A decision made from experience rather than projection.
costs: The old plan, and the time spent building it, is now a sunk cost.

nextSteps: Write down what would have changed your mind, so the next decision is not a fresh guess.
failurePoints: Treating a changed mind as wasted time and returning to the plan out of consistency.
